extracted.intended_audience: federal agency staff, regulated entities, stakeholders, and members of the public interested in U.S. federal rulemaking and information collection review
extracted.subtask_short: OIRA rulemaking and information collection review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on OIRA's role, procedures, and standards for review of agency regulatory actions and information collection requests under the APA, Executive Orders 12866 and 13563, and the Paperwork Reduction Act. Includes definitions, thresholds, timelines, disclosure rules, and evaluation criteria for agencies and commenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide public notice and seek comment (APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) generally requires agencies to provide public notice and seek comment prior to enacting new regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies typically publish a proposed rule in the Federal Register to solicit public comment; after considering public feedback and making changes where appropriate, they publish a final rule in the Federal Register with an effective date. The agency must describe and respond to the public comments it received when issuing a final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must describe and respond to public comments in final rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In issuing a final rule, the agency must describe and respond to the public comments it received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rules should explain how public comments were considered and what, if any, revisions were made in response to comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulation is a general statement issued by an agency, board, or commission that has the force and effect of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress often grants agencies authority or discretion to issue regulations; federal regulations specify details and requirements necessary to implement and enforce legislation enacted by Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA coordination role for significant regulatory actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 12866 assigns OIRA responsibility for coordinating interagency Executive Branch review of significant regulations before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA review ensures agencies comply with EO 12866 principles, incorporate public comment, consider alternatives, and analyze costs and benefits. For all significant regulatory actions, the Executive Order requires OIRA review before the actions take effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory analysis requirement under EO 12866
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 12866 requires agencies to assess both the costs and the benefits of the intended regulation and, to the extent permitted by law, propose or adopt a regulation only upon a reasoned determination that the benefits justify the costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must provide an explanation of the need for the regulatory action and an assessment of potential costs and benefits; other statutes (e.g., Regulatory Flexibility Act, Unfunded Mandates Reform Act) also require evaluation of costs and benefits for certain rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and standards for regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analysis is a tool agencies use to anticipate and evaluate the likely consequences of rules, including both costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposes include: (1) determining if benefits justify costs, (2) promoting accountability to the public, and (3) identifying which alternatives produce the highest net benefits. Careful analysis can show less or more stringent options, or creative alternatives. EO 12866 states agencies 'shall assess both the costs and the benefits' and recognize that some costs/benefits are difficult to quantify.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-4 guidance for regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB's Circular A-4 defines good regulatory analysis and standardizes measurement and reporting of benefits and costs of Federal regulatory actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular A-4 (latest guidance referenced: November 2023) assists agencies in performing high-quality regulatory analyses; OMB subjected a draft to peer review and solicited public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13563 principles for regulatory decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 13563 elaborates principles to guide regulatory decisionmaking, emphasizing public health and safety while promoting economic growth, and directing agencies to consider costs and benefits, including values difficult to quantify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five principles highlighted: (1) promote public participation (make documents available on regulations.gov and engage stakeholders before rulemaking), (2) reduce redundant/inconsistent/overlapping requirements by harmonizing rules, (3) identify flexible approaches (e.g., warnings, disclosures) to reduce burdens, (4) promote scientific integrity, and (5) produce plans to engage in retrospective analysis of existing significant regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'significant regulatory actions'
rubrics_metrics.description: Under EO 12866 (as amended), OIRA determines which regulatory actions are 'significant' and thus subject to interagency review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant regulatory actions are those that: (a) have an annual effect on the economy of $200 million or more (adjusted every 3 years), or adversely affect the economy, a sector, productivity, competition, jobs, environment, public health or safety, or governments/communities; (b) create serious inconsistency or interfere with another agency's actions; (c) materially alter the budgetary impact of entitlements, grants, fees, or loans or rights/obligations of recipients; or (d) raise legal or policy issues for which centralized review would further the President's priorities or EO principles (as authorized by the Administrator). The EO requires significant actions to be reviewed by OIRA and for agencies to provide explanation and cost-benefit assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'economically significant' regulatory actions
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset of OIRA-designated significant actions: 'economically significant' if likely to have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or otherwise materially affect the economy or other specified areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For economically significant regulations, the Executive Order directs agencies to provide a more detailed assessment of likely benefits and costs, including quantification, and to analyze potentially effective and reasonably feasible alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review period limits and extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The period for OIRA review is limited by EO 12866 to 90 days; there is no minimum period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review period may be extended indefinitely by the head of the rulemaking agency; alternatively, the OMB Director may extend review on a one-time basis for no more than 30 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for OIRA to 'return' an agency rule
rubrics_metrics.description: During review, the OIRA Administrator may send a letter returning the rule for reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Returns may occur if the rule is not compatible with the law; the agency's analysis is inadequate; the regulation is not justified by the analysis; the rule is inconsistent with EO 12866 principles or the President's policies/priorities; or the rule unnecessarily conflicts with other Executive Branch regulations or efforts. A return explains why further consideration would be beneficial and does not necessarily imply OIRA or OMB opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency withdrawal of a rule during OIRA review
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may withdraw its rule from OIRA review at any time and choose not to move forward or to resubmit after further consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interested parties may contact the agency with questions regarding specific withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA disclosure and transparency policies for meetings and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA makes public all substantive communications with any party outside the Executive Branch concerning regulatory actions under review and keeps a log of meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Administrator or designee meets with outside parties, the subject, date, and participants are disclosed on Reginfo.gov. Any written material received from outside parties on rules under review is placed on the OIRA website. After a regulatory action is published in the Federal Register, OIRA will make publicly available certain documents exchanged between OIRA and the rulemaking agency during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices for outside parties to influence OIRA review
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to participate in rulemaking is to submit comments directly to the agency during the proposed rule stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also: view the Federal Register for notices seeking public comments; file comments via regulations.gov; parties may provide written comments to the OIRA Administrator on actions under review and may request meetings (via EO 12866 Meeting Request page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft documents under OIRA review are deliberative and not public
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft documents under review are considered deliberative and are not available for public release during review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain documents exchanged between OIRA and the agency may be made public after the regulatory action is published in the Federal Register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Dashboard categories (types of regulatory actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reginfo.gov's Regulatory Dashboard displays types of regulatory actions under OIRA review: Notice, Pre-rule, Proposed rule, Final rule, Interim Final Rule, Direct Final Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions provided: Notice (announces new programs/policies); Pre-rule (solicit comment on initiating rulemaking); Proposed rule (proposes/regulatory changes and solicits comment); Final rule (agency responds to comments and issues final rule); Interim Final Rule (issued under statutory provisions allowing effect soon after publication, often with post-publication comment); Direct Final Rule (used for uncontroversial rules without a post-publication comment period).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory description availability depends on Unified Agenda submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions and abstracts of draft regulations undergoing OIRA review are provided by agencies via bi-annual Unified Agenda submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an individual rule's information is blank on the Regulatory Dashboard, it is because the agency did not provide descriptive information in its Unified Agenda entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIN (Regulation Identifier Number) use and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A RIN (Regulation Identifier Number) is assigned by OMB's electronic docketing system to identify each regulatory action listed in the Unified Agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB has asked agencies to include RINs in the headings of their Rule and Proposed Rule documents in the Federal Register to make it easier to track publication history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) requirements for information collections
rubrics_metrics.description: The PRA provides the statutory framework for the Federal government's collection, use, and dissemination of information and requires agencies to take specific steps before requiring or requesting information from the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals include minimizing paperwork burdens and ensuring maximum utility of collected information. Steps include seeking public comment on proposed information collections and submitting proposed collections to OMB for review and approval. PRA applies to collections using identical questions posed to, or reporting/recordkeeping requirements imposed on, ten or more 'persons' (individuals, businesses, and governments) and applies to voluntary and mandatory collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'information' under the PRA
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB's PRA regulation defines 'information' as 'any statement or estimate of fact or opinion, regardless of form or format,...' including forms, written reports, surveys, recordkeeping requirements, and third-party or public disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad definition covers numeric, graphic, narrative forms, oral or maintained on any media.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICR (Information Collection Request) process to obtain OMB approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Process: agency develops an information collection; publishes a Federal Register notice with 60 days for public comment; considers comments and makes changes as appropriate; submits the ICR to OMB and publishes a second Federal Register notice announcing OMB review and providing an additional 30 days for comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After review and consideration of public comments, OIRA approves the collection or takes other actions (approval, improperly submitted, withdrawn, disapproval). Under certain circumstances, an 'emergency' review may be requested with an explanation and requirement to consult members of the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions OIRA can take on agency ICRs
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA can: Approval, Improperly Submitted, Withdrawn, and Disapproval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA can approve collections for up to three years and may approve with or without change. For ICRs related to proposed rules, OMB may 'file comment' instructing the agency to resubmit the ICR at the final stage. An ICR returned as improperly submitted fails procedural requirements. If OIRA disapproves an ICR, the agency may not proceed with the collection and 'no person shall be subject to any penalty for failing to comply.'

rubrics_metrics.name: What OMB evaluates during review of proposed collections
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB evaluates whether the collection is necessary for the proper performance of the agency's functions (practical utility); minimizes Federal information collection burden (especially on those most adversely affected); and maximizes the practical utility/public benefit of information collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA also reviews consistency with applicable laws, regulations, and policies related to privacy, confidentiality, security, information quality, and statistical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: How the public can participate in information collection review
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public are encouraged to monitor Federal Register notices on agency information collections and provide feedback; the ICR Dashboard shows collections under review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments can be submitted to sponsoring agencies and to OIRA during the first 30 days of the information collection review via Reginfo.gov (View ICR - Agency Submission page 'Comment' button). Interested parties may contact agencies to submit comments outside the Federal Register timeframe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions and consequences for submitting Confidential Business Information (CBI) via Reginfo.gov
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not submit information whose disclosure is restricted by statute (trade secrets, commercial or financial information) to www.reginfo.gov because comments submitted through the site cannot be claimed as CBI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments submitted through the website will waive any CBI claims for the information submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: How comments submitted through Reginfo.gov are handled and disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments submitted through Reginfo.gov are maintained in ROCIS and OIRA is considered the official custodian of the comment; by providing comments you consent to their use and consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments submitted online will not be publicly disclosed on Reginfo.gov until OIRA concludes review. Any PII included in comments or attached files will be provided to OIRA and may be publicly disclosed on Reginfo.gov when OIRA's review is completed. Contact information provided with comments submitted online will not be publicly disclosed on Reginfo.gov and may only be used by OIRA. Reginfo.gov offers public data in XML that may include commenter name if included in agency-posted submissions; third parties may use the XML to build applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICR Dashboard categories (types of information collection requests)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICR Dashboard displays seven types of ICRs: New collection; Revision; Extension without change; Reinstatement without change; Reinstatement with change; Existing collection in use without OMB Control Number; Discontinue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: Revision = substantive revision to currently approved collection requiring public comment when significant; Extension without change = extend approval at least every three years via Federal Register notice; Reinstatement categories allow reuse of previous collections; 'Existing collection in use without OMB Control Number' requests approval for collections begun without prior approval; Discontinue requests termination of approval. OMB also handles non-material/technical changes without requiring public comment.
